passages.title: Ceide Fields
content: 📌 Céide Fields
An important Neolithic archaeological site in north-west Ireland
Discovery

In the 1930s, a schoolteacher concluded that the stones beneath the peat were parts of [ _____ ].His [ _____ ] later became an archaeologist and began a formal study of the location:
- iron probes adapted a local technique for finding [ _____ ] hidden in the bog
- carbon dating subsequently confirmed the site's Neolithic age.Artefacts remain in excellent condition because the peat contains very little [ _____ ].
Neolithic farmers

Their homes were [ _____ ] in design and included an opening in the roof.New practices and technology included:
- preparing food inside
- using pots for storage and as [ _____ ].One field could provide enough grazing for a large [ _____ ].The absence of animal shelters suggests that livestock remained outside during the [ _____ ].
Reasons farming ended
lower [ _____ ] qualitya rise in the amount of [ _____ ]
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a student giving a presentation about the Sade Fields, a prehistoric site in the North West of Ireland. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Today I'm going to describe the Sade Fields in North West Ireland.

[01:01] AUDIO: It is one of the world's most extensive Neolithic landscapes. I visited it recently and saw some of the archaeological work that is still taking place there. The site came to attention during the 1930s through a local schoolteacher called Patrick Caulfield. People cutting into the bog kept striking lines of stone below the surface.

[01:25] AUDIO: Caulfield worked out that these stones formed walls. As the peat had grown over them, the structures clearly had to be extremely old. He contacted the National Museum in Dublin and asked for the place to be examined, but his suggestion was dismissed. Proper investigation began about 40 years later.

[01:47] AUDIO: By then, Patrick's son Seamus had qualified as an archaeologist and decided to study the area himself. He pushed long iron probes down through the peat to trace the stone formations. Local people had traditionally used the same technique to find fuel buried in the bog. Subsequent carbon dating showed that the settlement was more than 5,000 years old and was Ireland's largest known Neolithic site.

[02:19] AUDIO: The bog has protected the remains remarkably well. It consists largely of water, so dead grasses and heather do not break down completely and instead build up in layers. The peat is acidic, but the main reason objects survive is that almost no oxygen reaches them. This process also depends on frequent wet weather.

[02:44] AUDIO: At least 175 rainy days are needed annually, while this part of Ireland receives about 225. Life at Sade seems to have remained peaceful and stable for several hundred years. Neolithic communities were larger than earlier ones, and several homes were often arranged around a shared building. Because these people lived in permanent settlements, their houses could be more substantial.

[03:16] AUDIO: It is sometimes assumed that the dwellings were circular, but they were actually rectangular. A small opening in the roof let smoke out, suggesting that these farmers were among the first people in Ireland to prepare food indoors. Pottery was another technology the settlers introduced. Pieces of Neolithic vessels have been recovered both at Sade and elsewhere in Ireland.

[03:44] AUDIO: The pots had several purposes. They stored food, of course, but people could also put a little fat inside and light it, turning the vessels into lamps. Archaeologists think most of the enclosed fields were paddocks where animals grazed. Each plot appears to have been big enough to maintain an extended family.

[04:06] AUDIO: The farmers may have moved animals from one area to another so that plants were not eaten too heavily and had time to grow again. Grazing was probably carried on throughout the year because no buildings had been found where livestock could have been kept during the winter. This settled way of life then appears to have ended quite suddenly. Several changes may explain why.

[04:33] AUDIO: Intensive farming and crop rotation gradually reduced the quality of the soil so agriculture was eventually abandoned. The climate also shifted. After a fairly dry period, conditions became much wetter and there was considerably more rain. Those wetter conditions allowed the bog that covers the landscape today to develop.
[04:58] AUDIO: So now I'd like to show you some ...

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a woman asking her friend Coleman about a guitar group he has recently joined. First you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:51] WOMAN: Hi Coleman, how are things?
[00:53] COLEMAN: Fine, thanks.
[00:54] WOMAN: I wanted to speak to you because Josh mentioned that you'd joined a guitar group. It sounds interesting and I'd really like to learn to play.
[01:03] COLEMAN: Why not come with me? I'm sure the group can take one more person.
[01:09] WOMAN: Really? Who teaches the classes?
[01:11] COLEMAN: His official role is the coordinator. His name is Gary Mathieson.
[01:16] WOMAN: I'll write that down. Gary, how is his surname spelt?
[01:21] COLEMAN: M-A-T-H-I-E-S-O-N Got it, thanks. He's retired now, but he's very friendly and used to perform with several bands.
[01:32] WOMAN: How long have you been attending?
[01:34] COLEMAN: For about a month.
[01:35] WOMAN: Could you already play before you joined?
[01:38] COLEMAN: Only a handful of chords. Nothing more than that.
[01:41] WOMAN: I'm worried everyone there will be more capable than I am.

[01:45] COLEMAN: I had exactly the same concern. When I first phoned Gary, he explained that the class was for beginners. I still expected the others to be ahead of me. But once I arrived, I discovered we were all equally inexperienced.
[02:02] WOMAN: That makes me feel better. Where does the group meet?
[02:06] COLEMAN: When I enrolled, the sessions were held at Gary's home. As membership increased though, he booked a room at the college in town. I much prefer the new venue.
[02:16] WOMAN: I know the college. I took tap dancing lessons there during secondary school, although I haven't visited for years. Which road is it on? Lock Street?
[02:28] COLEMAN: It's a little farther on, at the end of New Street. Close to the city roundabout.
[02:34] WOMAN: Yes, I remember now.
[02:36] COLEMAN: The group uses room T-347 on the first floor.
[02:41] WOMAN: And when are the meetings? Are they at the weekend?

[02:43] COLEMAN: They're on Thursday mornings. We previously began at 10.30, which was convenient for me. But the start time is now 11. The class before hours asked to keep the room for an extra half hour.
[02:58] WOMAN: I see. I'd love to join, but I don't own a guitar.
[03:02] COLEMAN: You could get a used one. A website called The Perfect Instrument sells guitars, violins, and similar items. So you should be able to find one there.
[03:17] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen carefully and answer questions 7 to 10.
[04:01] WOMAN: What normally happens in one of Gary's lessons?
[04:04] COLEMAN: He begins by asking everyone to tune their guitars, which takes roughly five minutes.
[04:11] WOMAN: Right.
[04:11] COLEMAN: Some learners use an app, while others tune by ear. Gary walks around helping them, and at the same time he outlines the plan for that day's lesson.
[04:21] WOMAN: Okay.
[04:23] COLEMAN: We then spend around 10 minutes practicing how to strum chords.
[04:27] WOMAN: Do you use those small things, plectrums?
[04:30] COLEMAN: No, we simply use our thumbs.
[04:33] WOMAN: That sounds easier.

[04:34] COLEMAN: Gary shows us where our fingers should go for each chord, and then we play together. Our timing is often so poor that we all start laughing. So Gary begins clapping to keep us together.
[04:48] WOMAN: Do you practice complete songs as well?
[04:50] COLEMAN: Yes. We work on at least one song that includes both lyrics and chords, and it's more difficult than it sounds.
[04:59] WOMAN: I can imagine.

[05:00] COLEMAN: That section lasts about 15 minutes. Gary often plays us a recording first. He then gives us the song, and if it contains an unfamiliar chord, we practice that before attempting the whole piece together at a very slow speed.
[05:18] WOMAN: Is finger-picking included?

[05:21] COLEMAN: That comes during the final 10-minute activity. We pick out individual notes from a simple tune Gary has composed. It still sounds challenging. It is, but people enjoy it because they can focus closely, and when everyone plays accurately, the result sounds impressive.
[05:39] COLEMAN: The uncomfortable part is that Gary sometimes asks us to perform one at a time. In other words, alone.
[05:48] WOMAN: That would make me nervous.
[05:50] COLEMAN: It did at first, but I'm accustomed to it now. During the last five minutes, Gary tells us what we should practice before the following session.
[05:59] WOMAN: Thanks, Coleman. I think I'll have a look at that website.
[06:05] NARRATOR: That is the end of part one.

passages.title: Working as a lifeboat volunteer
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Working as a lifeboat volunteer"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lifeboat volunteer called David talking about his work. First you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Becoming a lifeboat volunteer wasn't something I had planned when I moved from London to North Sea.

[00:55] AUDIO: I'd been employed as a website designer. The job itself was quite interesting, but living in the city didn't suit me. When I was younger, I'd been very keen on boats, so moving to the coast seemed like a good opportunity to take up that interest again in my spare time. Soon afterwards, I saw that the lifeboat institution needed volunteers and put in an application.

[01:21] AUDIO: You can't really miss North Sea's lifeboat station because it's among the biggest in the country. The building opened 15 years ago, paid for by a generous woman who had spent her whole life in the town. The institution is a charity, so it depends on gifts from individuals like her rather than receiving its money from the council or central government. My application included a medical examination and the doctor paid particular attention to my eyesight.

[01:55] AUDIO: I had once been short-sighted and used glasses, but laser surgery two years before had dealt with that. The test initially suggested that I might have trouble distinguishing colors. Fortunately, further checks showed there was no problem. Whenever the Coast Guard sends an alert, every crew member is contacted and heads straight to the station.

[02:21] AUDIO: We aim to arrive within five minutes. Once we're there, our goal is to launch the boat within a further six to eight minutes. We generally manage it, which we're proud of, since the national average is eight and a half minutes. As helmsmen, I steer the boat, but the role carries wider responsibility, too.

[02:44] AUDIO: I make sure all the necessary equipment is functioning properly, including special life jackets that can keep as many as four people afloat. Most importantly, I make the final judgment about whether conditions are safe enough for the lifeboat to leave. We almost always go, even when the weather is extremely bad. The role involves more than attending emergencies.

[03:11] AUDIO: People often fail to appreciate how quickly wind conditions at sea can alter, so I visit local youth organizations and sailing clubs to explain the dangers faced by sailors and swimmers when the weather deteriorates. Other volunteers arrange fundraising events and their contribution is essential, but that isn't my own area of work. Before you hear the rest of David's talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20.

[04:20] AUDIO: Our training never really stops. It concentrates on technical ability and handling the boat safely. The exercises have made me much more confident in extreme situations, so I'm able to think clearly instead of panicking. I was pleased that I had already completed a first aid course, because that helped with the casualty care sessions.

[04:44] AUDIO: We have also spent a considerable amount of time learning to handle ropes and tie knots, as those skills are fundamental. After my first year, I attended a specialist residential program lasting a week. One facility was a wave tank that could reproduce severe weather. It allowed us to practice surviving situations such as the lifeboat overturning during a storm at night.

[05:13] AUDIO: The course was demanding, but its purpose wasn't specifically to teach me how to lead other people. Since joining, I've responded to many different emergencies and the work remains enormously motivating. I enjoy understanding the technology and my experience in IT sometimes lets me assist the other volunteers. What matters most, though, is the crew itself.

[05:40] AUDIO: We operate as a close team, almost like a family, which makes it easier to get out of bed on a freezing, stormy night. In fact, winter call-outs can be the most rewarding. Accidents are often more serious then, so you can see how much your actions affect the final result. So if any of you listening are interested...

passages.title: Challenges in Footwear Recycling
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Challenges in Footwear Recycling"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students, Bella and Don, discussing footwear recycling for a presentation. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24.
[00:52] BELLA: Hi, Don. Did you receive the article about recycling footwear that I sent you?
[00:57] DON: Yes, I've got it here and I've read through it.
[00:59] BELLA: Do you think it will work as the subject of our presentation?

[01:04] DON: Before reading the article, I was doubtful. Footwear recycling sounded interesting, but I thought the subject might be too narrow. I assumed people simply put shoes in recycling bins, and then the shoes went to charity shops, leaving us with very little to discuss.
[01:24] BELLA: But the process is much more complicated than that.
[01:27] DON: I understand that now, and I'd like to investigate it further.
[01:32] BELLA: Good.
[01:33] DON: One fact that was new to me was the huge number of trainers that are recycled.
[01:38] BELLA: That makes sense because many young people wear trainers constantly now. They're more popular than conventional shoes.
[01:46] DON: True, and they seem very durable. But I think trainers look too informal with the school uniform, so I don't feel they're suitable for school.
[01:55] BELLA: I disagree. Some styles look quite smart on students, certainly smarter than a worn-out, untidy pair of shoes.
[02:04] DON: Do you normally keep your shoes for a long time?

[02:07] BELLA: I do. I often save old pairs for messy tasks, such as cleaning my bicycle. Though I have to admit that I've recycled shoes that were still in good condition. They still fitted and weren't unfashionable.
[02:21] BELLA: I simply stopped liking how they looked on me.
[02:24] DON: That's rather wasteful, isn't it? It's probably common because shoppers have so many choices. The article also reported that footwear sales have risen dramatically in recent years.
[02:37] BELLA: That didn't surprise me.
[02:39] DON: What puzzled me was the next statistic. The proportion of footwear being recycled has dropped to 6%, whereas it used to be 11%. I couldn't understand why it had fallen.
[02:53] BELLA: It's because some donated footwear never completes the recycling process. If shoes can't be sold again for one reason or another, the recycling center rejects them.
[03:07] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen carefully and answer questions 25 to 30.
[03:51] BELLA: Let's identify some examples from the article of footwear that the recycling center refused.
[03:57] DON: There are several in the interview with the recycling manager. Here's the relevant section.
[04:03] BELLA: Let's begin with the women's high-heeled shoes. What did the manager say about them?

[04:09] DON: They were probably costly. They were made of beige suede and seemed to have been worn only once. However, that single outing must have been in a very wet field, because the heels were heavily covered in mud and grass. They were simply too dirty to sell again.
[04:28] BELLA: All right. What was the problem with the leather ankle boots?
[04:32] DON: Their heels were worn, but that wasn't why they were rejected. One boot had become much paler than the other, probably after being left in sunlight, so the colors no longer matched.
[04:46] BELLA: I see. Next came the red baby shoes.
[04:49] DON: Yes.

[04:50] BELLA: People are instructed to fasten a pair together before placing it in a recycling bin, but many don't do that. The staff might have expected to find the missing shoe, but they never did. It was unfortunate, because the shoe they had was clearly brand new.
[05:08] DON: The trainers were interesting too. The manager said they looked as if a marathon runner had used them.
[05:15] BELLA: Weren't they rejected because the stitching had split?
[05:19] DON: Not quite. The sole of one trainer had worn so thin under the foot that there was a hole large enough to push a finger through.
[05:28] BELLA: Those examples would be useful in our presentation. They help explain why 90% of the shoes taken to recycling bins or centers eventually end up in landfill.
[05:41] DON: What did you think of the manager's project to prevent that waste by assembling new shoes from usable parts of old ones?

[05:48] BELLA: It seemed promising. With so many discarded shoes, I expected the team to find enough components to match. Still, I wasn't surprised that customers rejected the result. Personally, I'd worry about germs in secondhand footwear.

[06:07] BELLA: But hygiene wasn't the reason people refused to buy them. The project failed because the two shoes in each newly assembled pair weren't completely identical. The team did manage to send the shoes abroad, though.
[06:22] DON: That's another issue we should cover.
[06:23] BELLA: I used to think about the subject only in terms of my own recycling habits. I hadn't considered the broader system or everything that happens after shoes leave a collection point.
[06:36] DON: The process is far less straightforward than it appears, and presenting it from this different perspective will give us a fresh angle.
[06:45] BELLA: Exactly. So let's discuss...

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a student giving a presentation about tardigrades. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. For my project on invertebrate animals, I decided to investigate tardigrades.

[00:54] AUDIO: They are microscopic, or more accurately, almost microscopic, creatures belonging to the phylum tardigrata. Scientists have identified well over a thousand species. Most measure between 0.05 and 1 millimeter, although the largest can reach 1.2 millimeters. Tardigrades are often referred to as water bears.

[01:17] AUDIO: The word water reflects the environment in which they do best, while bear describes the way they move. Another common name is moss piglet. Inspired by their appearance when seen from the front, they were first recorded in Germany in 1773 by Johann Goethe, who later gave the group its scientific name. Although the species are numerous, they share several basic features.

[01:48] AUDIO: Their body is short and rounded, rather like a small barrel, and is divided into four sections. Each section normally carries a pair of legs. Most species have between four and eight pointed claws at the end of each leg. A few have no claws at all.

[02:06] AUDIO: Instead, they possess discs that use suction, allowing them to attach themselves to surfaces or hold prey. Inside the body, there are no lungs or other organs for breathing. A liquid fills the body cavity and transports both blood and oxygen. The head can appear flattened, and some websites even call it cute, though that is hardly a scientific description.

[02:33] AUDIO: Its mouth resembles a tube. This can extend outwards and expose sharp tooth-like structures called stilets, which pierce plant or animal cells. Tardigrades occur worldwide in many habitats. They are frequently found on the bed of a lake, on different kinds of vegetation, or anywhere that stays very damp.

[02:58] AUDIO: Research has shown how resilient they are. They can survive radiation and enormous pressure, as well as temperatures below minus 200 degrees Celsius and above 148 degrees. Some researchers suggest that tardigrades might remain alive even after humans disappeared, perhaps surviving an asteroid strike. When their surroundings become dangerously dry, they enter cryptobiosis.

[03:30] AUDIO: They pull in their head and legs and curl into a tiny ball known as a tun. That's T-U-N. Their metabolism then falls to under 1% of its normal rate. They may remain like this for decades, yet after water returns, they can become active again within hours.

[03:52] AUDIO: During cryptobiosis, a special protein prevents damage to their DNA. In 2016, scientists revived two specimens that had remained as tons for over 30 years. A much older claim from 1948 involved a tone said to be 120 years old, but nobody has successfully repeated that result. Experiments are now being conducted in space to establish how many days tardigrades can survive there.

[04:23] AUDIO: The confirmed record, as far as I know is 10 days, turning to diet, tardigrades live by taking in liquids. Despite having tooth-like stilets, they do not chew. They draw juice from moss and obtain fluid from seaweed. Certain species also feed on other tardigrades, whether from a different species or their own.

[04:47] AUDIO: That may be less surprising when we remember that their bodies consist mainly of liquid and have a gel-like coating. Finally, there is their conservation status. Tardigrades are thought to have existed for around half a billion years and to have survived five mass extinctions. The International Union for Conservation of Nature has not formally assessed them, and they do not appear on endangered lists.
[05:17] AUDIO: In fact, some scientists describe their populations as thriving. Does anyone have any questions? That is the end of part 4.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear Leon and Shannon discussing places to buy food near Shannon's new flat. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:48] LEON: Hi Shannon, how are you getting on in the new flat?
[00:51] SHANNON: Very well, thanks.
[00:52] LEON: It looks as though you're heading out to do some shopping.
[00:56] SHANNON: I am. Two of my cousins are staying for a few days, so I need to cook for them.
[01:00] LEON: You'll find several good food shops in Kite Place, the district beside the harbor.
[01:07] SHANNON: Great. I'll locate it on my map.
[01:09] LEON: What kind of food are you looking for?
[01:11] SHANNON: Neither cousin eats meat, although they're both keen on fish.
[01:16] LEON: In that case, the fish market there is excellent.
[01:19] SHANNON: Where exactly is it?
[01:21] LEON: Go to the far end of Kite Place, cross the bridge, and you'll see it on the right.
[01:27] SHANNON: Is it open throughout the day?
[01:28] LEON: It stays open until four, but some products sell out, so I wouldn't leave it until closing time.
[01:36] SHANNON: I definitely don't want to miss what I need.
[01:39] LEON: You'll be alright if you arrive by three thirty. It's only eleven now, so there's no rush.
[01:45] SHANNON: Good.
[01:45] LEON: Will you need vegetables as well?
[01:48] SHANNON: Yes, and I'd rather not buy everything wrapped in plastic at the supermarket.
[01:53] LEON: There's a lovely organic shop nearby. Its name is a flower.
[01:58] SHANNON: I've got it.
[01:59] LEON: It's called Rose.
[02:01] SHANNON: That's a pleasant name.
[02:02] LEON: It has vegetables, and quite a few other things too.
[02:06] SHANNON: How do I find it?

[02:08] LEON: When you reach the market, look left for a large gray building. It was probably a warehouse once. There's a restaurant upstairs and two shops on the ground floor, one on either side of the entrance. Rose is the shop on the left.
[02:23] SHANNON: That sounds straightforward.
[02:26] LEON: And there's a large sign out on the pavement, so it's hard to miss.
[02:30] SHANNON: Fine. If I still need anything, I suppose I'll have to use the supermarket.
[02:35] LEON: You should find everything there. A minibus goes to it as well. It's purple, and its route number is two hundred eighty-nine.
[02:44] SHANNON: Thanks. That's really useful.
[02:48] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions seven to ten. Now listen and answer questions seven to ten.
[03:31] LEON: What are you planning to buy at the fish market? The salmon is usually good, and so is the shellfish.
[03:38] SHANNON: I'm thinking of making a curry, and I'll need roughly twelve prawns for it.
[03:43] LEON: They should have plenty.
[03:45] SHANNON: Good.
[03:46] LEON: Have you ever eaten samphire?
[03:48] SHANNON: No. What is it?
[03:50] LEON: It's a kind of seaweed. You buy a handful and fry it in butter. It tastes wonderful.
[03:56] SHANNON: I may give that a try. How do you spell the name?
[04:00] LEON: S-A-M-P-H-I-R-E.
[04:05] SHANNON: Thanks. I enjoy trying unfamiliar food.
[04:09] LEON: So do I.
[04:10] SHANNON: At the organic shop, I'll see which beans are available, and I'd like to pick up some fruit for dessert.
[04:16] LEON: What about a mango?
[04:18] SHANNON: They can be disappointing when they aren't ripe. I'd rather have a melon, and it will serve more people.
[04:24] LEON: That makes sense. The shopkeeper also stocks plenty of spices for curries, as well as ingredients such as coconut.
[04:33] SHANNON: Excellent. I'll take a look.
[04:36] LEON: Anything else?
[04:37] SHANNON: Bread isn't an obvious match for curry, but I like having some on the table anyway.
[04:42] LEON: The bakery makes all its own bread and offers several kinds. I usually choose the brown loaf.
[04:50] SHANNON: That sounds good.
[04:51] LEON: It sells more than bread, too.
[04:53] SHANNON: Do they have cakes? Chocolate cake is my favorite.
[04:57] LEON: Not chocolate cake, but there are lots of tarts. The strawberry ones are the best.
[05:03] SHANNON: Perfect.

passages.title: Festival workshops
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Festival workshops"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a radio presenter interviewing Jenny Morgan, the organiser of a children's book festival. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. The children's book festival will be back very soon, and festival organiser Jenny Morgan is here to explain this year's programme.

[01:03] AUDIO: Jenny, what can families look forward to? As always, there will be five busy days of events for children, with writers travelling from many parts of the country to take part. Let me describe some of the workshops. Superheroes is a particularly special session where deaf children can talk about their experiences of reading with Madeleine Gordon, an author who also has a hearing impairment.

[01:31] AUDIO: Just Do It is a hands-on workshop run by the popular illustrator Mark Keene. He will guide the group through an imaginary adventure to distant places, and children who enjoy acting will be able to take part in role play. Count on Me offers an engaging exploration of friendship specifically for 13 and 14-year-olds. The group will examine friendships in familiar books and compare them with relationships in their own lives.

[02:01] AUDIO: Speak Up belongs to a workshop series about mental health. Through creative writing, children will describe occasions when young people feel lonely. Research has shown that loneliness can occur even when children are at home with their families. Jump for Joy is Nina Karan's warm, best-selling tale about a girl's journey to visit family members in India.

[02:25] AUDIO: The book recently won a gold medal at the Waterford Awards, and Nina herself will help participants celebrate the idea of joy by writing a poem. Finally, Sticks and Stones is an attractive picture book for younger readers. It follows a community arranging an African-Caribbean festival so that local children can discover their Jamaican heritage. The workshop will include music with opportunities to play steel drums.

[02:54] AUDIO: It is likely to fill quickly, so early booking is advisable. Before you hear the rest of the program, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Thank you, Jenny.

[03:45] AUDIO: Those sessions sound fascinating. Is there one book you would particularly recommend to our listeners? Choosing one is difficult, but Alive and Kicking deserves attention. The writer is not famous because this is her first book, which makes its quality even more remarkable.

[04:04] AUDIO: It takes the form of a teenage boy's diary after he moves from Somalia to the UK. The story examines immigration and serious difficulties at school, including the language barrier. Books on such themes are often rather sad, but this one made me laugh until I cried. The pictures are simple black and white stick drawings showing the boy with friends and teachers, not colorful illustrations.

[04:33] AUDIO: Each diary entry also ends with the new English words he has learned that day, which could broaden children's vocabulary. My own children would probably like that. What guidance would you give parents who want their children to read more? Parents ask me that frequently.

[04:52] AUDIO: Children face so many distractions that reading time can be difficult to protect. I recommend sitting with your child and sharing books. Many adults stop reading aloud as soon as a child can read alone, but they should continue. Hearing more demanding books helps build vocabulary.

[05:12] AUDIO: When parents cannot do this, audiobooks are a useful alternative and often encourage children to read the same titles afterwards. Parents should also notice whether a child keeps choosing one genre, since that may become repetitive, and then introduce different writers and types of book. A librarian can suggest suitable choices. That's extremely helpful, Jenny.

When parents cannot do this, audiobooks are a useful alternat"
explanation.step3: ❓ Câu hỏi : Which TWO recommendations does Jenny give parents about children's reading? ✅ Đáp án đúng : B. Let children use audiobooks E. Stop reading aloud once children can read independently ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Đoạn người dẫn bắt đầu hỏi về lời khuyên dành cho phụ huynh với tín hiệu như “What guidance would you give parents who want their children to read more?” . ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Trước khi nghe, hãy gạch chân các từ khóa recommendations , parents , và children's reading . Sau đó, tập trung nghe các động từ mang tính khuyên nhủ như recommend , should , useful alternative . Jenny nói: “Many adults stop reading aloud ... but they should continue.” Điều này cho thấy phụ huynh không nên dừng việc đọc thành tiếng quá sớm. Vì vậy, nếu đá
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: Let children use audiobooks.

passages.title: Science experiment for Year 12 students
content: 📌 Experimental procedure
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two trainee teachers, Claire and Jake, discussing a science experiment for year 12 students. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
[00:52] CLARE: Hi, Jake. How is the practical teaching going?
[00:55] JAKE: It is more demanding than I expected. Although some of my classes are excellent. What about yours?
[01:03] CLARE: Not very well. I'm having real difficulty with my year 12 science group.
[01:08] JAKE: Is their behavior hard to manage?

[01:11] CLARE: Discipline is not really the problem. They simply cannot see how science connects with everyday life, and that is frustrating. They listen, and their results in last week's test were reasonable, but they show almost no genuine interest.
[01:27] JAKE: I see.

[01:28] CLARE: For my teaching placement, I also have to plan an experiment for them. I considered a project on children's diets, perhaps asking pupils to record their meals and comparing that information with their health.

[01:43] JAKE: The food records would be manageable, but you would also need medical information about the children. Families might object because of confidentiality. The findings could be valuable if you obtain the data. Yet, getting it would probably be difficult.
[02:00] CLARE: That is true.
[02:00] JAKE: Have you considered an experiment with animals instead?
[02:05] CLARE: Would the students find that distressing?
[02:08] JAKE: The animals would not need to suffer. You could simply feed them a particular diet and observe the effects.
[02:16] CLARE: Would permission be difficult to obtain?
[02:19] JAKE: You would submit a short plan and complete a form, but the approval process is fairly simple.
[02:26] CLARE: Even if a diet changed in animals' health, though, we could not assume that people would respond in the same way.
[02:34] JAKE: Exactly, but every experiment has limits, so that issue cannot be removed entirely.
[02:40] CLARE: Fair enough? Which animals would be suitable for studying diet? Mice?
[02:46] JAKE: Yes, specially bred laboratory mice. What precise question would the experiment investigate?
[02:52] CLARE: Something related to nutrition. Perhaps the effect of supplements, such as additional iron or protein on health.
[03:01] JAKE: That covers too much. You could narrow it to one supplement, perhaps examining how sugar affects the mice.
[03:09] CLARE: Actually, it may be better to ask whether mice regulate how much they eat.
[03:14] JAKE: You mean what they do when extra sugar is available, even though they do not need it?
[03:19] CLARE: Yes. Would they consume it or choose not to?
[03:23] JAKE: Good. A later study could introduce another variable. Some mice might have a wheel and be able to exercise, while the others remain inactive.
[03:32] CLARE: I could also repeat the trial with another food or a different genetic strain of mouse. But varying the amount of exercise sounds more interesting, so I may develop that idea.
[03:46] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
[04:30] CLARE: Can I describe a possible procedure for the experiment using a sugar supplement?
[04:36] JAKE: Of course. I carried out a similar study when I was at college.
[04:40] CLARE: Excellent. How many mice should I use?
[04:42] JAKE: Around 12, all of them young, rather than a mixture of young and old animals.
[04:49] CLARE: I would divide them equally into two groups of six. How could I distinguish one group from the other? I thought of tags or some other kind of mark.
[05:00] JAKE: Food coloring would work and would not harm them.
[05:03] CLARE: Good. Each group would then be kept in a separate cage. Group A would be the control group and receive only ordinary commercial mouse food. Is that easy to buy?
[05:16] JAKE: Yes, it is sold as dry pellets.
[05:19] CLARE: Group B would receive the identical food with additional sugar.
[05:24] JAKE: Would you give them sugar on its own?
[05:26] CLARE: No, it would probably be better to mix the sugar into something such as cereal.
[05:32] JAKE: You should weigh the mice once a week using an electronic scale.
[05:35] CLARE: We cannot hold them on the scale because that would alter the measurement.
[05:40] JAKE: Right. Put each mouse in a weighing chamber so it cannot escape. That sounds specialized, but a plastic box with holes in the lid will do.
[05:50] CLARE: Once we have recorded each mouse's weight gain, we can calculate the mean for both groups and the standard deviation. Then decide how to continue. The students should enjoy this.
[06:03] JAKE: Yes. There is one other point.

transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear part of a lecture about microplastics and their effects on wildlife, soil, and plants. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. In this lecture, I'll be discussing microplastics.

[00:53] AUDIO: These are fragments of plastic measuring less than 5 millimeters. People have become much more aware of the enormous volume of plastic waste in the environment, from large discarded objects to particles too small to see. Plastic in the oceans has attracted a great deal of attention, but much less is understood about microplastics in fresh water and especially in soil. They reach the environment by several routes.

[01:22] AUDIO: Whenever synthetic clothing goes through a wash cycle, threads and minute fibers come loose and enter the water system. Larger plastic items already in the environment gradually fragment into microscopic particles. Industrial waste is another source, while vehicle tires also wear away as cars and lorries move over road surfaces. Studies involving fish and other animals have already shown several effects.

[01:51] AUDIO: Small creatures may suffer damage to their mouths. Their feeding can also be disrupted when plastic particles become trapped in the digestive system. It may be surprising, but people probably consume microplastics as well. They have been identified in bottled water and in water taken directly from the tap.

[02:15] AUDIO: Researchers have also found them in salt and in many varieties of seafood. Even so, there is still no conclusive evidence that microplastics seriously damage human health. Nevertheless, laws in a number of countries, including the UK, stop manufacturers from adding plastic microbeads to shower gels, facial cleansers and toothpaste. Estimating how much microplastic is present in soil is extremely difficult because the particles are not easy to detect.

[02:49] AUDIO: We do know that some travel through the air and are deposited by rain. In addition, many fertilizers used by farmers and gardeners contain microplastics. A research team at Anglia Ruskin University in Cambridge investigated how microplastics affect the digestive tracts of earthworms. These creatures live in topsoil and are vital to agriculture.

[03:14] AUDIO: As they feed, they mix nutrients through the earth, which helps to make it fertile. The researchers wanted to discover whether putting microplastics into soil and then having earthworms ingest them would reduce soil quality and ultimately restrict plant growth. The answer was clearly yes. They added three forms of microplastic to soil and planted perennial ryegrass.

[03:44] AUDIO: The materials included biodegradable PLA and conventional high-density polyethylene, or HDPE, and the worms then consumed the particles. The earthworms lost weight rapidly. Fewer ryegrass seeds than usual germinated because the worms could no longer perform their normal role in maintaining fertile soil. The researchers also recorded an increase in the amount of acid in the soil, which they linked mainly to particles from HDPE plastic.

[04:18] AUDIO: The study's conclusions are worth reading, and the full reference is included in the notes for the end of this session. In summary, the authors argue that soil should be understood as a natural process rather than as an inactive substance. It depends on decaying and dead material continually passing through earthworms. When microplastics impoverish the soil, the damage extends beyond ecosystems to society as a whole.

transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear a supervisor called Kaeden explaining a new employee's first-day arrangements at a supermarket. First, you have some time to look at questions one to six. Now listen carefully and answer questions one to six.
[00:49] KAEDEN: Morning, Charlotte. I am Kaeden, one of the supervisors here. Welcome aboard.
[00:55] CHARLOTTE: Thanks, Aiden.
[00:56] KAEDEN: Nearly. It's Kaeden. K-A-E-D-E-N. People often miss the first letter, so it's worth knowing the spelling.
[01:09] CHARLOTTE: Caden. Right, I'll remember that.
[01:12] KAEDEN: Good. There are a few practical things to deal with before I show you today's jobs.
[01:19] CHARLOTTE: My email said I should report to the front desk with my appointment letter and collect a staff badge.
[01:26] KAEDEN: That's correct. You'll need the badge to enter the staff-only areas. After that, come to the staff room with me. You can leave your coat and bag in whichever locker is free.
[01:40] CHARLOTTE: Does each locker have a key?
[01:42] KAEDEN: Yes. Keep it during your shift, then leave it in the lock when you finish, so the next person can use it.
[01:52] CHARLOTTE: Fine.
[01:53] KAEDEN: You must also visit human resources and ask for Tiffany.
[01:58] CHARLOTTE: I brought my passport as requested. She needs the number from it, doesn't she?
[02:03] KAEDEN: Yes. An identity card would also be acceptable. But your passport is perfect.
[02:11] CHARLOTTE: I don't have an ID card anyway.
[02:13] KAEDEN: Tiffany will also issue your uniform. There are several sizes, so tell her which one fits. I can't come with you because I need to deal with a faulty bread slicer.
[02:26] CHARLOTTE: Is HR close to the staff room?
[02:30] KAEDEN: The staff room is on the first floor. HR is two levels above it on the third floor. Use the stairs just outside the staff room.
[02:40] CHARLOTTE: Got it.
[02:41] KAEDEN: When you're finished there, meet me in the bakery section.
[02:46] CHARLOTTE: I'm looking forward to starting.
[02:48] KAEDEN: Before we split up, save my mobile number in case you can't find me.
[02:53] CHARLOTTE: Ready.
[03:01] CHARLOTTE: I've saved it.
[03:05] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7-10. Now listen and answer questions 7-10.

[03:48] KAEDEN: Your work today covers three areas. The bakery, the sushi take-away counter, and the meat and fish counters. In the bakery, begin by checking the sell-by dates on bread and cakes. Anything dated today needs a replacement price label.
[04:04] CHARLOTTE: And if I find something carrying yesterday's date, should I dispose of it?
[04:09] KAEDEN: Yes. Although the daily checks mean that's unlikely. For items dated today, use a yellow label and place it beside the original price.
[04:22] CHARLOTTE: Understood.
[04:23] KAEDEN: Next, move to the sushi counter.
[04:26] CHARLOTTE: Will I be making the food boxes?
[04:29] KAEDEN: Not on your first day. You're only supporting the regular staff.
[04:35] CHARLOTTE: All right.

[04:36] KAEDEN: At one end of the counter, you'll notice stacks of flat cardboard cartons. Directly underneath, we store the plastic boxes. Those run out quickly, so bring more from the store room whenever the supply gets low.
[04:53] CHARLOTTE: Is restocking all I do there?
[04:55] KAEDEN: No. Wipe the food preparation surface and clean the sink as well. The cloths and cleaning spray are beside it.
[05:05] CHARLOTTE: That makes sense.
[05:08] KAEDEN: One warning. Don't wash any knives. You need safety training before handling sharp equipment.
[05:16] CHARLOTTE: What should I do if knives have been left there?
[05:19] KAEDEN: Ask a trained colleague to put them in the dishwasher.
[05:23] CHARLOTTE: Thanks. I want to make sure I follow the rules.
[05:26] KAEDEN: You will. Finally, at the meat and fish counters, clean the customer serving area, including the weighing scales.
[05:36] CHARLOTTE: Anything else in that section?
[05:38] KAEDEN: The fish is displayed on ice. When it begins to melt, collect a fresh supply from the cold room.
[05:47] CHARLOTTE: The counter staff wear hats. Do I need one too?

passages.title: Training programmes for new runners
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 2: "Training programmes for new runners"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a running coach called Liz talking about training programs for beginners and her local running club. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen and answer questions 11 to 14. Hello, I'm Liz Fuller, a coach at Compton Park Runners Club.

[00:53] AUDIO: Welcome to the podcast. If you're considering taking up running, today's episode should help you get started. You'll find plenty of online plans designed to take beginners gradually towards a 5km run. Many are well structured.

[01:10] AUDIO: People of every age use them, and they're popular because the instructions are straightforward and the workload isn't extreme. Even so, one standard plan cannot suit everybody. Someone with a health issue such as asthma or a heart condition may need a program adjusted to their circumstances because most plans assume average health and fitness. They also offer little individual support.

[01:40] AUDIO: If a runner has a question about a personal difficulty, there may be nobody available to answer it. Here are two suggestions I give beginners. You may have heard that you should move extremely slowly until you become fitter, but going too slowly can actually hold back improvement. Choose a pace that feels manageable, record your time, and try to improve it gradually.

[02:11] AUDIO: I also recommend listening to music. It distracts you from tiredness and helps you settle into a rhythm. That is often more useful than running with a friend, since beginners can become competitive. Whether you train in the morning or evening is a personal choice.

[02:31] AUDIO: Consistency matters more. At the start, two runs each week are sufficient. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.

[03:23] AUDIO: People delay joining our club for several reasons. They may lack confidence, believe they dislike running, or struggle to make time. Sari joined two years ago when she was 40. She had enjoyed running at school, but she doubted whether she could keep up and feared being the slowest person in the group.

[03:45] AUDIO: The friendly welcome soon removed that concern. James was different. He simply disliked the idea of running. A friend eventually persuaded him to try one introductory session, and now he attends every week, even though his job is demanding.

[04:03] AUDIO: Leo's obstacle was his schedule. He thought a weekly commitment would be impossible to fit around work. When work became particularly stressful, however, he tried the club. Running now helps him relax, and he looks forward to each session.

[04:23] AUDIO: Mark had never regarded himself as athletic. After retiring, he decided that completing five kilometers would be a worthwhile challenge. His real difficulty was confidence. It took him months to contact us.

[04:39] AUDIO: Once he discovered other beginners of a similar age, he felt reassured. My own progress wasn't effortless either. I entered my first marathon at 37 after having two children. My husband had completed marathons for years, but I had never imagined joining him in one.

[05:00] AUDIO: So it wasn't a lifelong ambition, and he didn't pressure me. I finished in four hours, although halfway through, I came very close to giving up. The spectator's encouragement was what kept me going. Registering for an event can give new runners a useful target, whether the distance is 5 or 25 kilometers.

[05:24] AUDIO: My first 10-kilometer race came after six months, and it was harder than I expected, so I wouldn't advise copying that. After you have trained for a few weeks, though, it is worth signing up for a five-kilometer event scheduled a couple of months later. A few people race after only several practice runs, but most beginners should allow longer. Well, I hope that's given you enough to…
[05:56] AUDIO: That is the end of part two. You now have one minute to check your answers to part two.

questions.prompt: Match the statement/item with the correct option: "Ceri"

explanation.step1: Phân tích câu hỏi, xác định từ khóa và dự đoán thông tin theo Linearthinking.
explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "Sari joined two years ago when she was 40. She had enjoyed running at school, but she doubted whether she could keep up and feared being the slowest person in the group. The friendly welcome soon removed that concern."
explanation.step3: 📌 Tìm vị trí : Ceri ✅ Đáp án đúng : A ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Ngay sau câu “Ceri joined two years ago when she was 40.” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Cần nghe xem trở ngại ban đầu của Ceri là gì trước khi tham gia câu lạc bộ. Audio nói: “she doubted whether she could keep up” và “feared being the slowest person in the group” . Các cụm doubted , feared , slowest person đều cho thấy cô ấy thiếu tự tin về khả năng của mình. Vì vậy, đáp án đúng là A. a lack of confidence . 🧐 Lưu ý : ❌ B => Dễ nhầm nếu chỉ nghe cô ấy từng có băn khoăn khi tham gia, nhưng thực tế audio nói “She had enjoyed running at school” nên không phải ghét chạy . ❌ C => Đây là phương án dễ chọn nhầm nếu chỉ nhớ các lý do chung ở đầu bài, nhưng trong phần nói về Ceri , không có chi ti
explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: a lack of confidence

explanation.step3: 📌 Tìm vị trí : James ✅ Đáp án đúng : B ▶️ Bắt đầu nghe ở : Ngay khi nghe câu “James was different.” ☺️ Giải thích đáp án : Cần nghe xem trở ngại ban đầu của James là gì. explanation.step4: Đáp án chính xác: a dislike of running

questions.prompt: Match the statement/item with the correct option: "Leo"

Nghe tiếp: “He thought a weekly commitment would be impossible to fit around work.” → cụm impossible to fit around work nghĩa là anh ấy thấy không sắp xếp được thời gian quanh công việc. Câu tiếp theo “It took him months to contact us” càng củng cố rằng anh ấy thiếu tự tin , nên mất rất lâu mới dám liên hệ câu lạc bộ. 🧐 Lưu ý : ❌ B => Dễ nhầm nếu chỉ nghe câu “had never regarded himself as athletic” , nhưng câu này chỉ nói Mark không nghĩ mình có tố chất thể thao, không phải anh ấy ghét chạy. ❌ C => Đây là bẫy từ thông tin của Le

explanation.step2: Trích dẫn bài đọc / Audio: "My first 10-kilometer race came after six months, and it was harder than I expected, so I wouldn't advise copying that. Trong audio, Liz nói: “After you have trained for a few weeks…” → nghĩa là sau khi đã tập được vài tuần , người mới chạy nên đăng ký một sự kiện. Cần phân biệt rõ: sign up = đăng ký race date = ngày cuộc đua diễn ra Vì câu hỏi hỏi về khi nào nên đăng ký , không phải khi nào th

passages.title: Book Preservation
content: 🎧 HƯỚNG DẪN NGHE PART 3: "Book Preservation"

Bấm nút Play trên trình phát Audio phía trên để nghe bài thu âm chuẩn quốc tế và hoàn thành các câu hỏi ở cột bên phải. Bạn có thể chuyển sang tab "Transcript Hội Thoại" để đối chiếu lời thoại chi tiết và bấm giờ từng câu.
transcript: [00:00] NARRATOR: You will hear two students, Jane and Kieran, discussing how books should be cared for and arranged in a bookshop. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.
[00:52] KIERAN: You'll be leaving for your work placement in Denmark soon, won't you?
[00:56] JANE: Yes, and I'm excited. I've started packing my books so they can stay in storage while I'm away.
[01:02] KIERAN: I hope they survive the move without being damaged.
[01:07] JANE: They should. My grandfather works in a bookshop and he explained the safest way to pack them.
[01:14] KIERAN: Useful advice.
[01:16] JANE: He said the spine needs proper support. Otherwise, the pages can separate from the cover.
[01:22] KIERAN: That sounds like common sense.
[01:23] JANE: He also told me to lay books flat rather than stand them on their sides. If they bend and remain like that for a year, restoring their original shape is difficult.
[01:36] KIERAN: Again, the reason is obvious, though plenty of people don't make the effort to protect their books.
[01:44] JANE: Grandad also wishes publishers would choose stronger paper.
[01:48] KIERAN: The acid in paper is what causes deterioration, isn't it?
[01:52] JANE: Exactly. That's why older pages turn yellow. Several books he has given me are already showing that.
[02:00] KIERAN: Are you going to keep them?
[02:02] JANE: I probably shouldn't if they'll continue to decay, but I couldn't simply throw them away. They remind me of him.
[02:11] KIERAN: Even if a collector wouldn't consider them valuable, their personal meaning matters.
[02:17] JANE: Yes, I know I'd regret losing them.
[02:20] KIERAN: I was brought up to treat books carefully. It bothers me when students force paperbacks open and press so hard that the spine cracks.
[02:31] JANE: Paperbacks aren't made to last in the same way. Hardbacks are more robust.
[02:35] KIERAN: True, but people seem to value hardbacks less than they once did.
[02:41] JANE: Perhaps because they aren't usually treated as decorative objects. Many people no longer leave them visible on shelves.
[02:48] KIERAN: Which is a shame. When I visit someone and see a colourful book displayed on a table, I notice it immediately.
[02:57] JANE: Me too. A well-designed cover can be a piece of art in its own right.
[03:02] KIERAN: Taking a book off a shelf is another thing people often do badly.
[03:07] JANE: My grandfather says you should grip the whole top of the book. If there isn't enough space, move the neighbouring books aside so you can hold the entire cover.
[03:18] KIERAN: Did he teach you that recently?
[03:20] JANE: No. When I was little, he saw me tug a heavy volume out by the top of its spine. It dropped onto the floor and came apart.
[03:30] KIERAN: That must have made an impression.
[03:32] JANE: It did. I can still picture it clearly.
[03:36] KIERAN: Is there anything you especially enjoy about books?
[03:39] JANE: The smell of a brand new one.
[03:42] KIERAN: Same here.
[03:43] JANE: My parents used to tease me because I would hold new books close to my face before I even started reading.
[03:50] KIERAN: Unfortunately, newly printed books can be expensive.
[03:54] JANE: Yes. We're fortunate that we can afford to buy them. Many people can't.
[04:00] KIERAN: Your grandfather sells second-hand copies too, doesn't he?
[04:04] JANE: He does. They're more affordable. Although they don't have quite the same smell.
[04:13] NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.
[04:57] KIERAN: I'd love to own a shop like your grandfather's. How is his arranged?
[05:02] JANE: It's spacious with two main floors plus an attic and it carries almost every kind of book.
[05:09] KIERAN: I imagine first editions and other rare volumes are hidden away in the attic.
[05:16] JANE: You might expect that, but he wants customers to know they're available. They're displayed in the shop on a high shelf where a ladder is needed to reach them.
[05:25] KIERAN: That also makes them harder to steal.
[05:29] JANE: Exactly.
[05:30] KIERAN: What about books for children?
[05:32] JANE: He's keen to encourage young readers. He remembers sitting near the stairs with piles of books when he was a child.
[05:39] KIERAN: So are the children's titles kept by the stairs?
[05:42] JANE: No. He had a space designed especially for them on the ground floor. It has cushions so adults can sit there and read with toddlers.
[05:53] KIERAN: That sounds welcoming.
[05:55] JANE: There's also room for pushchairs near the entrance and a cafe for refreshments.
[06:00] KIERAN: With a shop that size, he must need storage.
[06:04] JANE: Yes. There's a storeroom at the back.
[06:07] KIERAN: Is that where he puts books nobody wants?
[06:09] JANE: No. He rarely discards anything. Unwanted books are left near the entrance so customers can take them without charge.
[06:18] KIERAN: A generous idea.
[06:20] JANE: The storeroom at the back is used for requested books. Orders from individuals and organisations are boxed there, away from the main shopping area.
[06:31] KIERAN: Did you buy your course books from him?
[06:34] JANE: Of course. He supplies several colleges. They used to be upstairs on the first floor. But after a university opened locally, he moved them down to attract students.
[06:46] KIERAN: Where are they now?
[06:48] JANE: They're within the cafe, on low shelves running around its walls.
[06:52] KIERAN: Very central.

passages.title: Tree planting
content: 📌 Tree planting
Reforestation projects should:

include a mixture of tree speciesavoid invasive species because they may enter into [ _____ ] with native speciescapture carbon, protect the environment and provide a sustainable source of [ _____ ] for local communitiesuse genetically diverse seeds to improve resistance to [ _____ ] and climate changerestore degraded land that was forested before, rather than land currently used for [ _____ ]
Large-scale reforestation projects
Planning decisions should be based on reliable, up-to-date [ _____ ].In Brazil, drones help identify forest threatened by illegal logging and the raising of [ _____ ].
Lampang Province, northern Thailand

Forest damaged by mining was restored with a range of native fig trees.These trees support wildlife and increase the [ _____ ] of recovery by attracting seed-dispersing animals and birds.For example, [ _____ ] began visiting the area within three rainy seasons.
Involving local communities

Destruction of Madagascar's mangroves made it harder for local people to earn a living from [ _____ ].The restoration project created jobs, rebuilt a healthy ecosystem and reduces the growing danger of [ _____ ].
transcript: [00:00] AUDIO: You will hear a lecturer talking about the principles of successful tree planting projects. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Tree planting has become a major theme in politics and public debate.

[00:55] AUDIO: It is regularly promoted as a simple response to the climate emergency and as a means for companies to balance out their carbon emissions. In reality, however, planting trees is far less straightforward than it may appear. Putting unsuitable trees in an unsuitable location can cause considerably more harm than benefit without helping either local people or the natural environment. Reforestation schemes are now being carried out on a vast scale in many countries, so choosing the appropriate trees is essential.

[01:34] AUDIO: Projects should use a mixture of species characteristic of the natural forest in that area, including rare and threatened varieties, so that a rich ecosystem can develop. Non-native trees that might become invasive should be excluded. Invasive species are a major factor in the worldwide biodiversity crisis. They often enter into competition with native species and can endanger their long-term survival.

[02:06] AUDIO: Restoring biodiversity in a way that maximizes carbon capture is central to reforestation, but a well-designed project should usually pursue several aims. Trees might be chosen to support wildlife, provide a sustainable supply of food for nearby communities, and maintain stable soil systems. A scheme is particularly successful when it achieves several of these aims without damaging local communities, native ecosystems, or vulnerable species. The survival and resilience of a restored forest also depend on seed selection.

[02:47] AUDIO: Seeds need a suitable level of genetic diversity, meaning enough variation within a species to help it survive. Low genetic diversity generally reduces a forest's resilience, leaving it more exposed to disease and less able to adjust to climate change. Selecting the right site matters just as much as selecting the right trees. Ideally, planting should take place on land that was once forested but is now in poor condition.

[03:20] AUDIO: Natural grasslands, savannas, and wetlands should be left alone because these ecosystems already make an important contribution to carbon capture. A site that can offer further benefits such as recreation may be preferable. Land currently used for agriculture should not be chosen because doing so often shifts deforestation to another area. Large reforestation programs require meticulous planning, and sound decisions about where planting should occur depend on reliable information.

[03:57] AUDIO: Detailed current maps that show the highest priority locations for intervention are therefore indispensable. Drones can also help specialists identify priorities and monitor damaged forest. In Brazil, for instance, this technology is being used to locate and measure parts of the Amazon threatened by human activities, particularly the raising of cattle and illegal logging. Lampang Province in northern Thailand provides a useful example of appropriate tree choice.

[04:33] AUDIO: A former forest site degraded by mining was restored through cooperation between a cement company and Chiang Mai University. After 60 cm of topsoil had been spread, 14 native tree species were planted, among them several kinds of fig. Figs are considered a keystone species because they play such an important part in sustaining wildlife populations. They are especially valuable in tropical reforestation because they increase the speed of recovery by drawing in birds and other animals, which then disperse seeds naturally.

[05:13] AUDIO: This supports diversity by encouraging the healthy return of many plant species. Unlike most fruit trees, figs produce fruit throughout the year, so they offer wildlife a dependable food source. At the Lampang site, monkeys began arriving to eat the figs after only three rainy seasons, and they spread seeds naturally in their droppings. Every reforestation project should also make a point of consulting local communities and involving them in decisions.

[05:46] AUDIO: The restoration of Madagascar's mangrove forests shows how a project can bring genuine community benefits. When the mangroves were destroyed, plant and animal life suffered badly. The damage also affected fishing, a major source of work for people in coastal settlements. The restoration program employed local residents to plant and care for new mangroves.

[06:14] AUDIO: Millions of trees have now been established, allowing a healthy aquatic ecosystem to return. The mangroves also provide protection against the growing danger of flooding linked to climate change. In addition, the local economy is more secure, and thousands more families can afford to send their children to school. One other important point to consider.
[06:41] AUDIO: That is the end of part four. You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
